     6	
     7	Trimesh is a pure Python (2.7-3.4+) library for loading and using [triangular meshes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_mesh) with an emphasis on watertight surfaces. The goal of the library is to provide a full featured and well tested Trimesh object which allows for easy manipulation and analysis, in the style of the Polygon object in the [Shapely library](https://github.com/Toblerity/Shapely).
     8	
     9	The API is mostly stable, but this should not be relied on and is not guaranteed: install a specific version if you plan on deploying something using trimesh.
    10	
    11	Pull requests are appreciated and responded to promptly! If you'd like to contribute, here is an [up to date list of potential enhancements](https://github.com/mikedh/trimesh/issues/199) although things not on that list are also welcome. Here are some [tips for writing mesh code in Python.](https://github.com/mikedh/trimesh/blob/master/trimesh/exchange/README.md)

    14	## Basic Installation
    15	
    16	Keeping `trimesh` easy to install is a core goal, thus the *only* hard dependency is [numpy](http://www.numpy.org/). Installing other packages adds functionality but is not required. For the easiest install with just numpy, `pip` can generally install `trimesh` cleanly on Windows, Linux, and OSX:
    17	
    18	```bash
    19	pip install trimesh
    20	```
    21	
    22	More functionality is available when soft dependencies are installed. This includes things like convex hulls (`scipy`), graph operations (`networkx`), faster ray queries (`pyembree`), vector path handling (`shapely` and `rtree`), preview windows (`pyglet`), faster cache checks (`xxhash`), etc. To install `trimesh` with the soft dependencies that generally install cleanly on Linux, OSX, and Windows using `pip`:
    23	```bash
    24	pip install trimesh[easy]
    25	```
    26	
    27	Further information is available in the [advanced installation documentation](https://trimsh.org/install.html).
    28	
    29	## Quick Start
    30	
    31	Here is an example of loading a mesh from file and colorizing its faces. Here is a nicely formatted
    32	[ipython notebook version](https://trimsh.org/examples/quick_start.html) of this example. Also check out the [cross section example](https://trimsh.org/examples/section.html) or possibly the [integration of a function over a mesh example](https://github.com/mikedh/trimesh/blob/master/examples/integrate.ipynb).
    33	
    34	```python
    35	import numpy as np
    36	import trimesh
    37	
    38	# attach to logger so trimesh messages will be printed to console
    39	trimesh.util.attach_to_log()
    40	
    41	# mesh objects can be created from existing faces and vertex data
    42	mesh = trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=[[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0]],
    43	                       faces=[[0, 1, 2]])
    44	
    45	# by default, Trimesh will do a light processing, which will
    46	# remove any NaN values and merge vertices that share position
    47	# if you want to not do this on load, you can pass `process=False`
    48	mesh = trimesh.Trimesh(vertices=[[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0]],
    49	                       faces=[[0, 1, 2]],
    50	                       process=False)
    51	
    52	# some formats represent multiple meshes with multiple instances
    53	# the loader tries to return the datatype which makes the most sense
    54	# which will for scene-like files will return a `trimesh.Scene` object.
    55	# if you *always* want a straight `trimesh.Trimesh` you can ask the
    56	# loader to "force" the result into a mesh through concatenation
    57	mesh = trimesh.load('models/CesiumMilkTruck.glb', force='mesh')
    58	
    59	# mesh objects can be loaded from a file name or from a buffer
    60	# you can pass any of the kwargs for the `Trimesh` constructor
    61	# to `trimesh.load`, including `process=False` if you would like
    62	# to preserve the original loaded data without merging vertices
    63	# STL files will be a soup of disconnected triangles without
    64	# merging vertices however and will not register as watertight
    65	mesh = trimesh.load('../models/featuretype.STL')
    66	
    67	# is the current mesh watertight?
    68	mesh.is_watertight
    69	
    70	# what's the euler number for the mesh?
    71	mesh.euler_number
    72	
    73	# the convex hull is another Trimesh object that is available as a property
    74	# lets compare the volume of our mesh with the volume of its convex hull
    75	print(mesh.volume / mesh.convex_hull.volume)
    76	
    77	# since the mesh is watertight, it means there is a
    78	# volumetric center of mass which we can set as the origin for our mesh
    79	mesh.vertices -= mesh.center_mass
    80	
    81	# what's the moment of inertia for the mesh?
    82	mesh.moment_inertia
    83	
    84	# if there are multiple bodies in the mesh we can split the mesh by
    85	# connected components of face adjacency
    86	# since this example mesh is a single watertight body we get a list of one mesh
    87	mesh.split()
    88	
    89	# facets are groups of coplanar adjacent faces
    90	# set each facet to a random color
    91	# colors are 8 bit RGBA by default (n, 4) np.uint8
    92	for facet in mesh.facets:
    93	    mesh.visual.face_colors[facet] = trimesh.visual.random_color()
    94	
    95	# preview mesh in an opengl window if you installed pyglet with pip
    96	mesh.show()
    97	
    98	# transform method can be passed a (4, 4) matrix and will cleanly apply the transform
    99	mesh.apply_transform(trimesh.transformations.random_rotation_matrix())
   100	
   101	# axis aligned bounding box is available
   102	mesh.bounding_box.extents
   103	
   104	# a minimum volume oriented bounding box also available
   105	# primitives are subclasses of Trimesh objects which automatically generate
   106	# faces and vertices from data stored in the 'primitive' attribute
   107	mesh.bounding_box_oriented.primitive.extents
   108	mesh.bounding_box_oriented.primitive.transform
   109	
   110	# show the mesh appended with its oriented bounding box
   111	# the bounding box is a trimesh.primitives.Box object, which subclasses
   112	# Trimesh and lazily evaluates to fill in vertices and faces when requested
   113	# (press w in viewer to see triangles)
   114	(mesh + mesh.bounding_box_oriented).show()
   115	
   116	# bounding spheres and bounding cylinders of meshes are also
   117	# available, and will be the minimum volume version of each
   118	# except in certain degenerate cases, where they will be no worse
   119	# than a least squares fit version of the primitive.
   120	print(mesh.bounding_box_oriented.volume,
   121	      mesh.bounding_cylinder.volume,
   122	      mesh.bounding_sphere.volume)
   123	
   124	```

   126	## Features
   127	
   128	* Import meshes from binary/ASCII STL, Wavefront OBJ, ASCII OFF, binary/ASCII PLY, GLTF/GLB 2.0, 3MF, XAML, 3DXML, etc.
   129	* Import and export 2D or 3D vector paths from/to DXF or SVG files
   130	* Import geometry files using the GMSH SDK if installed (BREP, STEP, IGES, INP, BDF, etc)
   131	* Export meshes as binary STL, binary PLY, ASCII OFF, OBJ, GLTF/GLB 2.0, COLLADA, etc.
   132	* Export meshes using the GMSH SDK if installed (Abaqus INP, Nastran BDF, etc)
   133	* Preview meshes using pyglet or in- line in jupyter notebooks using three.js
   134	* Automatic hashing of numpy arrays for change tracking using MD5, zlib CRC, or xxhash
   135	* Internal caching of computed values validated from hashes
   136	* Calculate face adjacencies, face angles, vertex defects, etc.
   137	* Calculate cross sections, i.e. the slicing operation used in 3D printing
   138	* Slice meshes with one or multiple arbitrary planes and return the resulting surface
   139	* Split mesh based on face connectivity using networkx, graph-tool, or scipy.sparse
   140	* Calculate mass properties, including volume, center of mass, moment of inertia, principal components of inertia vectors and components
   141	* Repair simple problems with triangle winding, normals, and quad/tri holes
   142	* Convex hulls of meshes
   143	* Compute rotation/translation/tessellation invariant identifier and find duplicate meshes
   144	* Determine if a mesh is watertight, convex, etc.
   145	* Uniformly sample the surface of a mesh
   146	* Ray-mesh queries including location, triangle index, etc.
   147	* Boolean operations on meshes (intersection, union, difference) using OpenSCAD or Blender as a back end. Note that mesh booleans in general are usually slow and unreliable
   148	* Voxelize watertight meshes
   149	* Volume mesh generation (TETgen) using Gmsh SDK
   150	* Smooth watertight meshes using laplacian smoothing algorithms (Classic, Taubin, Humphrey)
   151	* Subdivide faces of a mesh
   152	* Minimum volume oriented bounding boxes for meshes
   153	* Minimum volume bounding spheres
   154	* Symbolic integration of functions over triangles
   155	* Calculate nearest point on mesh surface and signed distance
   156	* Determine if a point lies inside or outside of a well constructed mesh using signed distance
   157	* Primitive objects (Box, Cylinder, Sphere, Extrusion) which are subclassed Trimesh objects and have all the same features (inertia, viewers, etc)
   158	* Simple scene graph and transform tree which can be rendered (pyglet window, three.js in a jupyter notebook, [pyrender](https://github.com/mmatl/pyrender)) or exported.
   159	* Many utility functions, like transforming points, unitizing vectors, aligning vectors, tracking numpy arrays for changes, grouping rows, etc.
   160	
   161	
   162	## Viewer
   163	
   164	Trimesh includes an optional `pyglet` based viewer for debugging and inspecting. In the mesh view window, opened with `mesh.show()`, the following commands can be used:
   165	
   166	* `mouse click + drag` rotates the view
   167	* `ctl + mouse click + drag` pans the view
   168	* `mouse wheel` zooms
   169	* `z` returns to the base view
   170	* `w` toggles wireframe mode
   171	* `c` toggles backface culling
   172	* `g` toggles an XY grid with Z set to lowest point
   173	* `a` toggles an XYZ-RGB axis marker between: off, at world frame, or at every frame and world, and at every frame
   174	* `f` toggles between fullscreen and windowed mode
   175	* `m` maximizes the window
   176	* `q` closes the window
   177	
   178	If called from inside a `jupyter` notebook, `mesh.show()` displays an in-line preview using `three.js` to display the mesh or scene.    194	## Which Mesh Format Should I Use?
   195	
   196	Quick recommendation: `GLB` or `PLY`. Every time you replace `OBJ` with `GLB` an angel gets its wings.
   197	
   198	If you want things like by-index faces, instancing, colors, textures, etc, `GLB` is a terrific choice. GLTF/GLB is an [extremely well specified](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/master/specification/2.0) modern format that is easy and fast to parse: it has a JSON header describing data in a binary blob. It has a simple hierarchical scene graph, a great looking modern physically based material system, support in [dozens-to-hundreds of libraries](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/issues/1058), and a [John Carmack endorsment](https://www.khronos.org/news/press/significant-gltf-momentum-for-efficient-transmission-of-3d-scenes-models). Note that GLTF is a large specification, and `trimesh` only supports a subset of features: loading basic geometry is supported, NOT supported are fancier things like animations, skeletons, etc.
   199	
   200	In the wild, `STL` is perhaps the most common format. `STL` files are extremely simple: it is basically just a list of triangles. They are robust and are a good choice for basic geometry. Binary `PLY` files are a good step up, as they support indexed faces and colors.
   201	
   202	Wavefront `OBJ` is also pretty common: unfortunately OBJ doesn't have a widely accepted specification so every importer and exporter implements things slightly differently, making it tough to support. It also allows unfortunate things like arbitrary sized polygons, has a face representation which is easy to mess up, references other files for materials and textures, arbitrarily interleaves data, and is slow to parse. Give `GLB` or `PLY` a try as an alternative!
